item.description:
Source: spectrum.ieee.org

Top Comment:

Aside: I think I need some help here.[0]

I remember reading Godel Escher Bach back in the day, and there is the parable of the record player between the tortoise and the rabbit. And the tortoise keeps building more and more secure record players that the rabbit keeps finding ways to break.

GEB then goes on to teach you that, no, in fact, you cannot have a perfectly secure system. Not just practically or economically, but even in theory, all systems are fundamentally breakable. GEB, after a lot of chapters (what a doorstop!) ties that parable into Godel's Incompleteness Theorem, and essentially proves that no, you can't make unbreakable things, as a fundamental point of logic.

So, when I look at all this, I see that yes, there is an economics point of view here, that fixing code is just expensive, like making a less and less breakable record player. And that AIs push that breaking and economics point much further along than what we have had.

But then I also see a lot of comments here that seem (to me) to be arguing that there is an unbreakable code out there.

Am I reading this right? Is there such a thing as 'perfect' code? Or is my outdated reading of GEB still valid or not?

[0]Note, I'm not a CS person, more a biophysics person.

item.title: Tell HN: Gemini trains on chat history, even for subscribers (personal accounts)
item.description:
Source: news.ycombinator.com

If you have a personal Google AI subscription, all your saved chat history in Gemini can be used for training and there is no way to opt out unless you turn off chat history or use temporary chat sessions. These chat transcripts may even be read by human reviewers. Although Google claims to disconnect them from your account when human-reviewed, they explicitly warn not to enter confidential information.

https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/16836988

“[Gemini app activity] is used to improve Google services for everyone, including by training generative AI models, if your Keep Activity setting is on.“

https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/13594961?hl=en#human_review

“A subset of chats are reviewed by human reviewers”

https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/13594961?hl=en#pn_retain_data

“Chats reviewed by human reviewers [...] are not deleted when you delete your activity. Instead, they are retained for up to three years.”

https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/13594961?hl=en#pn_data_usage

“Please don’t enter confidential information that you wouldn’t want a reviewer to see or Google to use to improve our services, including machine-learning technologies.”

To disable their training on your chat sessions, you need to turn off “Keep Activity” in Gemini’s settings. Turning that off means you’ll lose any chat sessions after 72 hours.

I learned this too late, thinking that having a paid subscription = not being turned into the product. Apparently paying is not enough.

Thank you to this user on HN for mentioning in another thread: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50355424

Top Comment:

"These chat transcripts may even be read by human reviewers."

PSA: This is true of all the frontier model providers even if you disable activity tracking. They are all constantly monitoring your interactions for problematic behavior.

item.title: North Korean fake job interview led to $6.3B Binance heist
item.description:
Source: www.theregister.com

Top Comment:

A lot of people are focusing on how irresponsible the engineer was about using the work computer. That's obviously an issue but the bigger failure mode to me is the Engineer C's container deployment token.

That's a huge red-flag. In a company of this size, the deployments should be via CI only. CI isn't just to increase the speed and reliability of deployments but also to provide a clean room to build the software! Even if it's a token that was copied and pasted temporarily, the systems in place should not have to require this type of 1. copy 2. paste 3. remember-to-delete the token from my PC.

Also, Binance should be paying for intrusion testing. Better to pay a trusted company to do this kind of thing instead of letting North Korea show you how it's done. I don't think this exact exploit path would have been found but I bet the intrusion testing would have figured out another way to use Engineer C's token.

item.title: Incident with Pull Requests, Git Operations and Issues
item.description:
Source: www.githubstatus.com

Top Comment:

What I find problematic, especially for teams that rely on GitOps and GitHub being (relatively) stable, is the fact that GitHub's status page can't be relied on. You arrive at the conclusion, "this must be GitHub," but the status page rejects the notion, and so you go digging. That can lead to a lot of toil and wasted time, in addition to sideways looks paired with comments like, "but status shows green."

A sick person with symptoms is clearly sick, but sometimes they're asymptomatic. That's what the GitHub status page has become. When it's red and showing problems, you know you have problems. When it's all green? You know you MIGHT have problems.

That can make outages like this harder to triage, since reality is a black box.
